lesson.title: Exhausting a Server One Half Open Handshake at a Time
lesson.summary: A SYN flood is a denial of service technique that exploits the TCP three way handshake by sending a large number of connection requests and never completing them, exhausting the resources a server sets aside for connections still in progress.
lesson.body:
The TCP three way handshake requires a server to do something specific the moment it receives a connection request: it allocates a small amount of memory to track that pending connection, sends back its own SYN-ACK, and then waits for the final ACK that completes the handshake. That allocation exists for a good reason, the server needs somewhere to keep the connection's state while it waits, but it also means that every half finished handshake ties up a small, limited resource on the server, and a server can only track so many half open connections at once before it runs out of room for new ones.

A SYN flood is exactly this DDoS technique aimed at that specific limited resource. The attacker sends a large volume of SYN packets, the first step of the handshake, often from spoofed source addresses so the server's SYN-ACK replies go nowhere useful and definitely never come back as a completed handshake, and then simply never sends the final ACK for any of them. Each of those unfinished handshakes sits in the server's connection table as a half open connection, consuming a slot. Send enough of them fast enough, and the server's table of pending connections fills up entirely. At that point, the server can no longer accept new SYN requests, including ones from legitimate users genuinely trying to connect, because there's no room left to track them. The service becomes unreachable not because a network link got saturated with raw traffic volume, but because one small, specific resource, the pending connection table, got exhausted, exactly the resource exhaustion style DDoS category described in the previous chapter.

Understanding this mechanism is what makes the standard defense make sense rather than feeling like an arbitrary trick. A technique called SYN cookies lets a server respond to a SYN with a SYN-ACK without allocating any connection state up front at all: the server encodes the information it would normally have stored into the sequence number of its own SYN-ACK reply, in a way it can verify later, and only actually allocates a connection table entry once the final ACK comes back and proves it. If the final ACK never arrives, as it never will for spoofed flood traffic, essentially nothing was ever committed on the server's side, so an attacker sending a flood of SYNs that never complete has no scarce resource left to exhaust. This is a clean illustration of a recurring defensive principle: rather than trying to filter out malicious traffic before it arrives, which is difficult when it's spoofed and looks superficially identical to a real request, redesign the protocol handling so the attack technique no longer has a resource left to consume.
